name: Network Economic-Effect Evidence

positioning.oneLineSummary: Tests whether maturing atomic networks improve monetization or unit economics through observable operating mechanisms.
positioning.productLabel: Economic-Effect Lens — based on Andrew Chen's public Cold Start materials

attribution.display: Based on Andrew Chen's public Cold Start materials

neutralParaphrase: Determine whether greater relevant participation improves an economic driver—such as match rate, utilization, conversion, take-rate durability, pricing, service cost, or required subsidy—and whether that improvement persists after incentives and mix effects are separated.

locator.value: Part IV, Chapters 24-25, PDF pp. 228-237; subsidy discussion, PDF pp. 167-168
Marketplace, economics, concentration, and network-effect metrics

requiredConditions: Atomic-network maturity and economic outcomes can be measured.
Gross economics can be reconciled with incentives, service costs, and participant payouts.

requiredEvidence.description: Revenue, gross profit, contribution, CAC, payback, utilization, and service costs by atomic-network maturity.
Specified pathway from density to match, conversion, utilization, pricing, take rate, cost, or subsidy.
Participant incentives, guarantees, discounts, manual operations, and off-ledger support.
Comparable economic cohorts across immature and mature atomic networks.

decisionQuestions: Which economic variable should improve as relevant density rises?
Does gross-profit or contribution improvement survive subsidy and service-cost reconciliation?
Is the effect repeated across atomic networks and participant sides?
Could mix, pricing, selection, or accounting policy explain the result?
positiveSignals: Mature networks reach better match, utilization, conversion, or contribution economics.
Required incentive per retained participant declines without quality loss.
Participant value and platform monetization improve together.
Economics reproduce in new networks after a measurable maturation period.
redFlags: GMV or bookings rise while contribution economics deteriorate.
Liquidity depends on permanent guarantees, discounts, or manual fulfillment.
Higher take rate weakens hard-side retention.
Aggregate margin improvement comes from geographic or customer mix.
disconfirmingEvidence: Dense networks require increasing subsidy or support.
The hard side captures all incremental economics or exits after monetization changes.
Unit economics are no better in mature networks.
Reported contribution omits incentives, support, fraud, refunds, or participant acquisition.
contraindications: Do not equate transaction volume with economic network effect.
Do not model subsidy disappearance without a demonstrated trajectory.
Do not assume pricing power if participants can multi-home or bypass the platform.

instructions: Specify the economic mechanism before reviewing the outcome.
Reconcile unit economics and all subsidies by network cohort.
Compare immature and mature networks and participant sides.
Test mix, pricing, accounting, and selection alternatives.
Conclude demonstrated, emerging, subsidy-dependent, contradicted, or insufficient.

deterministicRule.prohibition: The language model must not calculate unit economics, subsidy adjustment, or margin bridges.

sourceReliability.medium: Network-cohort model with partial ledger support.
sourceReliability.high: Audited or reconciled transaction, ledger, subsidy, and cohort data converge.

evidenceStrength.medium: A plausible economic relationship exists but subsidy or causality remains.
evidenceStrength.high: Repeated, subsidy-adjusted operating evidence supports the mechanism.

evidenceCoverage.medium: Core economics and some subsidies covered.
evidenceCoverage.high: Revenue, contribution, incentives, service cost, quality, cohorts, and participant distribution covered.

applicabilityConfidence.medium: Mechanism is plausible but immaterial or early.

empiricalQualifications: Accounting conventions and subsidies can obscure the effect.
Participant capture can limit platform value.

rights.notes: Public doctrine and affiliated metrics are neutrally paraphrased.

openIssues: Specify subsidy-adjusted economic templates by business model.
